Q1: Decision: Dispatch the Medic unit to Call A (Maple St, chest pain, 7.8). The 9.0 threshold is an escalation trigger for mutual aid and command notification, not a gate on dispatching at all. Holding the unit idle while a serious chest-pain call waits would cost lives; highest urgency wins the next unit, every time.
Q2: Decision: Dispatch the Engine to Call A (Pine Rd, kitchen fire, 8.4). A kitchen fire in an occupied structure scores highest at 8.4 and needs the engine now — the fact that neither call reaches 9.0 changes nothing about who gets the unit. Call B (dumpster fire, 7.9) waits in queue for the next available unit.
Q3: Decision: Dispatch the Ladder truck to Call A (1st St, person trapped on 3rd floor, 8.9). Both calls sit just below critical, but the principle is unchanged: the highest-scored waiting call gets the next unit regardless of threshold. A person trapped with smoke showing edges out the elevator rescue at 8.8, so Call A goes first.
Q4: Decision: Dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, diabetic emergency, 7.1). A conscious diabetic emergency outranks an event standby at 5.5 on honest urgency scoring. Units exist to serve scored calls, not to sit staged; the standby event does not justify holding.
Q5: Decision: Dispatch the Medic to Call A (River St, difficulty breathing, 8.1). The scores are nearly tied, but 8.1 is the higher score and breathing difficulty carries time sensitivity the hip-injury fall does not. The urgency score exists precisely as the tiebreaker for decisions like this.
Q6: Decision: Dispatch the Engine to Call A (Main St, vehicle fire, 6.8). It outscores Call B (brush fire near homes, 6.5), so it gets the unit. Accept the neighboring jurisdiction's mutual aid for Call B so neither call is left uncovered — the aid offer is a resource, not a reason to hold our own engine.
Q7: Decision: Dispatch the Battalion Chief to Call A (Park Ave, multi-vehicle accident, 7.5). It is the only call waiting and it specifically needs command oversight. There is no reason to hold the only command resource when a scored call is waiting; dispatch it.
Q8: Decision: Dispatch the Medic to Call A (Cedar Ln, stroke symptoms, 8.7). Highest-scored call, and the time-critical treatment window makes delay especially costly. Abdominal pain at 7.3 queues for the next unit. No call needs to hit 9.0 for the highest scorer to get dispatched.
Q9: Decision: Dispatch the Engine to Call A (Summit Dr, gas leak, 5.9). A gas leak with an evacuated home is a scored call waiting, and a 5.9 is a serious score — the threshold does not mean only 9.0+ calls deserve a response. Holding the engine with an empty queue is the naive default the principle rejects.
